item.content:encoded:
AlterNet’s headline casts Donald Trump as the victim of a geopolitical coup. The analysis it describes says almost the opposite: Jonathan V. Last, writing in The Bulwark, argues that Trump has made the United States a willing partner of authoritarian powers, allowing Vladimir Putin’s Russia and Xi Jinping’s China to gain American alignment without surrendering their relationship with Iran.

That is not a story about something done to Trump. It is an accusation about what Trump, as president, is doing with American power.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

From a loose slogan to an authoritarian partnership

Last begins with George W. Bush’s “Axis of Evil,” the label his administration applied in 2002 to Iraq, Iran and North Korea. Even on its own terms, Last writes, that grouping was incoherent. Iran and Iraq were enemies, while North Korea sold assistance to governments willing to pay. They were repressive states, but not a functioning alliance.

The more consequential alignment, in Last’s account, emerged later among Russia, China and Iran. By 2012, he argues, the three governments had spent years developing relationships intended to constrain liberal powers.

That distinction matters. Bush’s phrase bundled adversaries together for the political purposes of the War on Terror. Last is describing something more concrete: governments coordinating where their interests overlap, despite differences among them.

But he also revives Bush’s morally loaded terminology, which risks flattening distinct relationships into another sweeping civilizational camp. The useful question is not whether every government fits neatly inside an “evil” axis. It is how state power is being exercised, which partnerships it strengthens and whose interests those choices serve.

The charge against Trump

Last’s central claim is that Russia did not need to defeat the United States because it managed to “flip it.” He characterizes the Trump administration as a Putin-controlled regime and presents Trump’s reported meeting with Xi in Shenzhen that Thursday as the moment the new alignment would become visible.

“Putin and Xi” had effectively exchanged Iran for “Donald Trump’s America,” Last writes, calling the development “the most stunning geopolitical coup” ever. He further argues that Russia and China achieved this without abandoning Iran, even as, in his description, America was at war with it.

The supplied reporting does not detail the policies, agreements or concessions underlying that assessment. It does establish that Last’s argument concerns Trump’s use of the presidency, not Trump being personally duped or overpowered. His language is polemical, but the institutional structure is plain: the president controls the foreign-policy machinery of the United States. Putin and Xi may benefit from Trump’s decisions; they do not issue those decisions from the Oval Office.

Calling Trump the “victim” therefore redirects attention from the officeholder exercising American power to the foreign leaders allegedly profiting from it. That framing grants Trump passivity precisely where Last assigns him agency.

A headline that reverses the allegation

There is a legitimate argument to examine in Last’s commentary: whether Trump’s foreign policy weakens traditional liberal alliances while improving the strategic position of authoritarian governments. AlterNet’s account, however, supplies more invective than policy evidence. “Puppet regime” and “idiot president” communicate Last’s judgment; they do not, by themselves, demonstrate the mechanism of the alleged geopolitical realignment.

The headline makes the distortion worse. A president who chooses accommodation, alignment or deference is not necessarily the casualty of those choices. The country whose power he directs may bear the consequences. Allies may face them. People subjected to the strengthened reach of repressive governments may face them. But the reporting presented here does not establish Trump as the coup’s victim.

Last’s actual accusation is harsher: Trump is the means by which the supposed coup succeeds. If that accusation is to carry more than rhetorical force, it must rest on the president’s concrete decisions and their beneficiaries. The “victim” framing obscures exactly that chain of responsibility.

item.title: Senator rages at Trump nominee at live hearing: 'It’s absurd!'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand’s objection to Hung Cao, President Donald Trump’s nominee for Navy secretary, was not about decorum. It was about Cao’s attempt to recast eight suicide attempts aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln as evidence that the Navy’s support system worked. For an administration already accused of dismissing the sailors’ suffering and restricting congressional scrutiny, the language was more than callous: it converted institutional failure into a management success. The sailors endured
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand’s objection to Hung Cao, President Donald Trump’s nominee for Navy secretary, was not about decorum. It was about Cao’s attempt to recast eight suicide attempts aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln as evidence that the Navy’s support system worked. For an administration already accused of dismissing the sailors’ suffering and restricting congressional scrutiny, the language was more than callous: it converted institutional failure into a management success.

The sailors endured a 321-day deployment that was extended twice, according to AlterNet. Food ran low. One service member lost 45 pounds, Gillibrand said, while families sent care packages to keep those aboard fed, functioning and physically capable of doing their jobs. Against that record, Cao offered an extraordinary accounting.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

“You see, as eight suicide attempts, I see as eight suicide mitigations because of the chaplains we have on board, the deployment resiliency counselors, as well as mental health specialists,” he said. Cao added that carrier strike groups on deployment normally experience “about one or two suicides.”

That comparison does not lessen the severity of eight attempts. It reveals the standard Cao chose: not whether commanders subjected sailors to intolerable conditions, but whether those conditions produced fewer deaths than he implied might otherwise be expected.

Turning breakdown into a performance metric

Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, said Cao was “absolutely not” suited to lead the Navy. She accused him of displaying callousness and failing to understand the needs of deployed personnel.

“Literally calling suicide attempts mitigation. It’s absurd,” she said.

The absurdity lies in the institutional sleight of hand. Chaplains, counselors and mental-health specialists may have helped prevent deaths; Cao’s statement credits their intervention. But successful emergency intervention does not vindicate the conditions that created the emergency. Calling the attempts “mitigations” shifts attention from sailors driven to crisis toward an organization congratulating itself for catching some of them before they died.

It also reduces human suffering to an outcome on an administrative ledger. Under that logic, a sailor’s suicide attempt can become evidence of resilience programming rather than a warning about command decisions, deployment extensions, shortages and the cumulative strain imposed on the crew.

Gillibrand made the material conditions central to her criticism. Families were not merely offering comforts from home, by her account. They were sending supplies needed to keep service members alive and able to work. Cao’s framing asks those sailors and families to view the absence of completed suicides not as the narrow avoidance of catastrophe, but as proof that the institution performed well.

Denial above, exclusion around it

Gillibrand said she also intended to press Cao about Trump calling reports that service members were committing suicide “fake news” and about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s reported claim that the story was made up.

“How can he stand by Secretary Pete Hegseth, who said this was all made up?” she asked. “These are leaders who are not taking the sacrifice of our service members seriously, and that’s unacceptable.”

The administration’s posture, as described in the report, follows a recognizable progression: deny the damaging account, redefine the evidence that cannot be ignored, and restrict the opposition’s access to information needed for oversight. Host Peter Alexander noted that the administration and Defense Department had refused for months to brief Democrats about events. Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota reportedly acknowledged that Democrats had been excluded from classified discussions.

Gillibrand said she raised the matter directly with Rounds and called the exclusion “disgraceful.” Her question was properly aimed at the official controlling access: why was the Trump administration withholding a classified briefing from Democratic senators?

Classified information is not the personal property of a president, defense secretary or congressional majority. Cutting opposition lawmakers out of briefings weakens Congress’s ability to test official claims precisely when senior officials are disputing accounts of severe harm to service members. The exclusion does not establish what happened aboard the Abraham Lincoln, but it concentrates control over the story in the same executive branch whose conduct is under scrutiny.

Accountability deferred

Gillibrand called for Hegseth to face accountability for what she described as his inability to lead troops and establish policy supporting service members. She said she believed a new Congress would investigate his leadership and the treatment of personnel deployed around the world.

That leaves the immediate power imbalance intact. Sailors bore the prolonged deployment, food shortages and mental-health crisis. Their families supplied what they could from outside. Administration officials retained control over the Pentagon, its explanations and access to classified information. Cao, seeking authority over the Navy, responded to eight suicide attempts by renaming them.

Whether the interventions aboard the carrier prevented deaths is one question. Whether the people who imposed and managed those conditions should be allowed to count the resulting crises as institutional successes is another. Cao’s answer supplied Gillibrand’s objection for her: a nominee prepared to treat attempted suicides as favorable statistics is already speaking in the language institutions use to escape responsibility.

item.title: DOJ humiliated as judge jokes about Trump’s blabbing in revenge probe
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Chief Judge James Boasberg did not expose a Justice Department humiliation so much as a breakdown in the department’s excuse: the government wants secrecy for an investigation that President Donald Trump and senior administration officials have already discussed in public. At a Tuesday hearing, Boasberg considered whether to unseal records supporting the Oct. 12 search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington home. item.content:encoded:
Chief Judge James Boasberg did not expose a Justice Department humiliation so much as a breakdown in the department’s excuse: the government wants secrecy for an investigation that President Donald Trump and senior administration officials have already discussed in public. At a Tuesday hearing, Boasberg considered whether to unseal records supporting the Oct. 12 search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington home. He has not yet ordered the full warrant file released and indicated that substantial portions may remain sealed.

The revealing exchange came when a Justice Department lawyer said she could not control public remarks by Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the investigation’s focus. “Seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg replied, according to Politico reporter Kyle Cheney.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

That was a joke, but the institutional problem was not funny. The administration’s most powerful officials can publicize allegations against a political adversary while the department conducting the investigation asks a court to preserve secrecy around the evidence, witnesses and legal basis for its actions.

Public accusation, private justification

The New York Times, Judicial Watch and 14 press organizations have asked Boasberg to unseal the warrant used to search Omar’s home. The Justice Department argues that the warrant has not been fully executed. Boasberg questioned that characterization, distinguishing the October search from the government’s continuing review of the seized material.

That review involves the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause, which protects legislative work from executive intrusion. According to Boasberg, most of the briefing and prior orders address that protection. He described the remaining dispute as a set of “purely legal questions” concerning the privilege’s reach, its application in this case and the procedures the government must follow.

This distinction matters. Calling the warrant unexecuted allows the department to describe an already completed search as unfinished, potentially strengthening its argument for continued secrecy. Boasberg’s questioning stripped away that convenient blur: agents executed the search in October; the government is now sorting through what it took and confronting constitutional limits on its access.

The judge nevertheless identified legitimate interests in withholding some material. He said the 67-page application contains significant information about the investigation’s scope, along with witnesses whose identities and roles should not yet be revealed. He is considering a partial release, not indiscriminate disclosure.

That is a more consequential story than the headline’s spectacle of bureaucratic embarrassment. A judge is weighing public access against an active investigation and witness protection while policing the executive branch’s treatment of constitutionally protected legislative material.

A prosecution apparatus with political sponsorship

Federal investigators are examining alleged discrepancies in Omar’s financial disclosures and whether her father misstated her age in citizenship documents, AlterNet reported. The Justice Department has told the court that the investigation reaches “other individuals,” and a court filing said Attorney General Todd Blanche approved the warrant.

Omar denies wrongdoing and says the Trump administration is targeting her politically. No finding reported in the source establishes that she committed either financial or immigration fraud.

The administration has nonetheless supplied the investigation with an extraordinary punitive frame. Border czar Tom Homan has said Omar could face denaturalization and deportation if investigators uncover evidence of immigration fraud. The conditional language is important: Homan described what could follow a finding, not a result investigators have already reached. But the intervention still places the machinery of citizenship revocation and expulsion into public discussion before the reported allegations have been proved.

That is where power lies in this case. Omar can deny the claims and contest the search. The administration controls the Justice Department, federal investigators and immigration enforcement, while its leading officials possess an unmatched platform for broadcasting suspicion. When those officials speak, they do not act as detached commentators on a process beyond their reach. They lead the government operating that process.

The department lawyer may genuinely lack authority to silence the president or his senior officials. Her lack of control, however, is not the same thing as the administration lacking agency. It means the official defending secrecy in court is institutionally subordinate to people who can discuss the investigation publicly without bearing the immediate burden of reconciling those remarks with the government’s legal position.

Boasberg returns to the target list

The hearing also unfolded against the administration’s prior campaign against Boasberg. In March 2025, he temporarily blocked deportation flights carrying people the government alleged were Venezuelan gang members. Trump responded by calling him a “Radical Left Lunatic” and demanding his removal from the bench.

Sen. Eric Schmitt later proposed legislation branded the “Boasberg Act,” which would require random assignment of federal district court cases. Whatever policy argument its sponsors may make for random assignment, naming the proposal after a judge attacked by the president turns court administration into personalized political punishment.

Now Boasberg is reviewing a search approved at the highest level of the Justice Department and directed at one of Trump’s prominent political antagonists. His task is narrower than the surrounding political conflict: determine which records may be released, protect witnesses where warranted and resolve the Speech or Debate Clause questions raised by the government’s review.

The court has not decided the underlying allegations against Omar, and Boasberg’s quip did not do so either. What it exposed was the administration’s asymmetrical arrangement: senior officials can amplify an investigation’s accusations, threaten its most severe possible consequences and attack the judge supervising it, while the Justice Department arrives in court insisting that the supporting record must largely remain beyond public view.

item.title: Trump shifts legal strategy in golf course fight
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Justice Department is no longer concentrating on persuading Judge Ana Reyes to bless the Trump administration’s stated rationale for closing the East Potomac Park golf course. According to a joint status report filed Tuesday and described by Politico’s Josh Gerstein, government lawyers instead want to waive a preliminary-injunction hearing, finish briefing by Nov. 25 and obtain a ruling before a temporary restraining order expires Nov. 28. The shift would limit the time available to examine
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department is no longer concentrating on persuading Judge Ana Reyes to bless the Trump administration’s stated rationale for closing the East Potomac Park golf course. According to a joint status report filed Tuesday and described by Politico’s Josh Gerstein, government lawyers instead want to waive a preliminary-injunction hearing, finish briefing by Nov. 25 and obtain a ruling before a temporary restraining order expires Nov. 28. The shift would limit the time available to examine whether federal officials manufactured a safety justification after President Donald Trump had already ordered the course redeveloped.

The course closed Nov. 15. Trump’s plan would replace the inexpensive, heavily used public facility with a championship-level, PGA-style course occupying the island and capable of hosting official tournaments. That is not merely a redesign. It is a transfer of public space from ordinary Washington-area users—who have relied on its affordability and location for generations—to a prestige project dictated from the White House.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A deadline built around the administration’s timetable

The immediate dispute concerns how quickly Reyes should decide whether the government may keep part of East Potomac Park closed. Her temporary restraining order keeps the park open but excludes the golf course, leaving the administration’s central objective largely intact while the litigation proceeds. Over the weekend, the course gave away its training clubs, photographer Andrew Leyden reported, a practical sign that the shutdown was already being treated as more than a temporary interruption.

The administration argues that witness testimony and extended proceedings would waste time. Its preferred schedule would close written arguments before Thanksgiving and permit Reyes to rule before the restraining order lapses.

The plaintiffs want time to investigate. They are seeking testimony from contractors to compare what those parties were told with representations made by the Justice Department and White House. They also argue that the government’s compressed schedule would disrupt witnesses’ plans during the holiday week.

That procedural disagreement carries the substance of the case. The administration wants the judge to decide rapidly on the existing record; its opponents want to test how that record was constructed. Speed, under those circumstances, is not neutral. It benefits the institution that made the decision, terminated the existing operation and began defending the resulting closure.

Safety appeared after Trump’s directive

The administration has said the island needed to close because its seawall was submerged or collapsing. But according to AlterNet’s account, safety was not part of the government’s stated case until after Trump announced on Truth Social that the course would close Nov. 15 for redevelopment into a championship-level venue.

That chronology is why further testimony matters. The allegation is not simply that officials offered an unpersuasive explanation. The Justice Department has been accused of inventing a justification that would allow renovation work to begin without the required approval. Government lawyers dispute the court’s earlier finding that they acted in bad faith.

Reyes has already identified a more direct chain of responsibility. In her temporary restraining order, she found that the Park Service ended the existing operator’s role “so that it could close the Park to effectuate President Trump’s directive to begin work on the Fazio Design immediately.” She also rejected the notion that the absence of an operator was an independent problem confronting the government: federal officials had created that condition themselves.

The distinction is crucial. Bureaucracies often present the consequences of their own decisions as external constraints—there is no operator, the facility cannot function, closure is unavoidable. Reyes’s finding cuts through that misdirection. The Park Service removed the operator in service of the president’s redevelopment order and then faced the operational vacuum its decision produced.

A public course converted into a presidential project

The institutional power here is not held by the local golfers, runners or cyclists who use East Potomac Park. It belongs to the president who issued the directive, the Park Service that acted on it and the Justice Department now pressing the court to resolve the challenge before opponents can gather the testimony they say they need.

The proposed transformation also reveals whose interests count in the redevelopment. The existing course’s political value lies precisely in features a prestige project can erase: it is affordable, accessible and embedded in a larger public park. Trump’s plan would turn the entire island into a tournament-scale venue. The promised upgrade therefore carries a concrete loss, replacing broad everyday use with a facility designed around championship status and official events.

Whether the administration’s safety claims withstand scrutiny remains a matter for the court. But the reported sequence is already clear: Trump announced the closure and redevelopment; safety concerns entered the government’s explanation afterward; the Park Service terminated the operator; and the Justice Department now seeks a ruling without the evidentiary hearing opponents want. The government is asking the court to treat urgency as a reason to curtail scrutiny when that urgency arose from the government’s own rush to execute the president’s order.

item.title: Leaker reveals how Trump 'deliberately' gutted essential US cyber defenses
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Miles Taylor, a former senior Homeland Security official in Donald Trump’s first administration, says the president has systematically weakened the federal government’s ability to defend essential infrastructure from cyberattack. His warning rests on two reported decisions: the Trump administration loosened oversight of artificial intelligence systems that can be weaponized against digital infrastructure, and after returning to office in 2025, it hollowed out the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure
item.content:encoded:
Miles Taylor, a former senior Homeland Security official in Donald Trump’s first administration, says the president has systematically weakened the federal government’s ability to defend essential infrastructure from cyberattack. His warning rests on two reported decisions: the Trump administration loosened oversight of artificial intelligence systems that can be weaponized against digital infrastructure, and after returning to office in 2025, it hollowed out the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency just as AI was making cyber threats more dangerous.

Taylor’s assessment is not an official finding or a prediction with a fixed timetable. But the institutional damage he describes is concrete: CISA has lost roughly one-third of its workforce, remains without a Senate-confirmed director, and faces a proposed $700 million cut. The people with the power to reverse that deterioration are not hackers, civil servants or frightened consumers. They are the president and the officials carrying out his agenda.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An agency punished after contradicting Trump

Taylor helped draft the law that created CISA and later watched Trump sign it. Congress designed the agency to serve as the federal government’s principal domestic cyber-defense operation, protecting the systems that keep elections, communications, transportation and commerce functioning.

The agency’s political trouble began when it performed that mission in a way Trump found personally inconvenient. After the 2020 election, CISA’s first director rejected Trump’s false narrative that the election had been stolen and described it as the most secure in US history. Trump fired him by tweet.

That sequence matters. The dispute was not over whether CISA had failed to protect the election. The agency’s offense was contradicting the president’s preferred account of an election he lost. Taylor says Trump subsequently dismantled the programs built to defend the country, then “shredded the agency” after returning to power in 2025.

This is institutional retaliation with a public cost. A cyber-defense agency cannot function as intended if its leaders and employees understand that accurate assessments may be punished whenever they collide with presidential claims. Weakening its staff and leadership compounds that pressure: it reduces both the agency’s technical capacity and its ability to speak with authority inside the government.

Technical capacity traded for political obedience

Current and former CISA employees told Taylor that the agency is now “a shell of its former self.” One described a threadbare staff, with only a small number of employees able to understand advanced AI developments, and said the White House would not listen even if the agency tried to act.

That account exposes the practical consequence of governing through loyalty tests. Cybersecurity depends on specialized expertise, sustained preparation and officials willing to report unwelcome facts. Trump’s treatment of CISA, as Taylor describes it, has degraded all three.

The administration’s approach to AI adds another layer of exposure. Taylor argues that Trump gave the industry a “hall pass” by removing safety rules and permitting reckless deployment. He attributes that policy to the influence of technology executives who cultivated Trump through money and flattery and were rewarded with diminished oversight.

The source material does not identify the particular regulations, executives or transactions behind that characterization, so it does not establish a specific quid pro quo. The documented political structure is nevertheless clear: the administration controls federal safeguards, industry stands to benefit from their removal, and the public bears the risk when powerful systems are deployed without adequate defenses.

A warning, not proof of a particular attack

AlterNet notes that aviation, communications, banking and commercial systems had suffered major problems during the preceding week, with cyberattackers blamed for some of them. The reporting does not establish that every disruption was a cyberattack, that AI caused the incidents, or that CISA’s reduced capacity allowed them to occur.

Taylor’s broader warning is prospective. He says Americans may not grasp the weakness of federal defenses until attacks produce rolling outages, block access to cash, disrupt travel and public services, create shortages or shut down electricity. Those are scenarios, not reported outcomes. His claim is that an administration responsible for preparing against them has made preparedness substantially worse.

He compares the government’s vulnerability to the failures preceding the September 11 attacks, calling the present lack of readiness “vastly worse.” That is an extraordinary assessment from a former official, but it remains his assessment. The staffing losses, leadership vacuum and proposed budget reduction give it more substance than a generic warning, even if they cannot establish when an attack will occur or how severe it would be.

“On our own” is a consequence of government policy

Former Trump White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham wrote that she no longer believed or trusted the people running the government. Taylor went further, warning against accepting assurances from the White House or Homeland Security that the threat is under control.

Personal distrust from former officials is not itself evidence of an imminent cyberattack. The sharper indictment lies in what Taylor reports about the machinery of government: an agency created to protect the public contradicted Trump, its leader was fired, and its workforce and authority were then diminished during a period of escalating technical risk.

Taylor says Americans are more “on our own” than they realize. If that is now true, it is not because cybersecurity somehow became too complicated for government. It is because officials with the authority to maintain the country’s defenses chose to strip capacity from the institution built for the job.

item.title: Ex-MSNBC host makes explosive plantation comparison about former network
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: MSNBC canceled Tiffany Cross’s Saturday morning program and declined to renew her contract in November 2022 after executives reportedly grew uneasy with commentary they considered too sharp for the network’s preferred style. Cross now describes the Black executive who dismissed her, then-MSNBC president Rashida Jones, as “more overseer than freedom fighter”—a plantation comparison aimed less at Jones’s identity than at the corporate function Cross says Jones performed. The distinction matters. C
item.content:encoded:
MSNBC canceled Tiffany Cross’s Saturday morning program and declined to renew her contract in November 2022 after executives reportedly grew uneasy with commentary they considered too sharp for the network’s preferred style. Cross now describes the Black executive who dismissed her, then-MSNBC president Rashida Jones, as “more overseer than freedom fighter”—a plantation comparison aimed less at Jones’s identity than at the corporate function Cross says Jones performed.

The distinction matters. Cross is not claiming that representation carries no value or that Jones lacked authority. She is arguing that putting a Black woman in charge did not alter the institution’s standards, incentives or capacity to punish a Black woman whose voice made executives uncomfortable. Jones held the formal power. MSNBC owned the platform. Cross lost her show.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Representation without institutional change

In an interview with Charles Blow for Forward, Cross challenged the assumption that a Black executive’s advancement necessarily translates into protection or solidarity for other Black employees.

“When I see someone reach the helm, the pinnacle of a career, and they look like me, it’s an, ‘Oh, your win is my win,’” Cross said, before asking whether Black professionals are sometimes celebrating “a Black version of one of them.”

When Blow asked whether that description applied to her former boss, Cross answered directly: “Oh, yes. 100% percent. Yeah, definitely.”

Her “overseer” remark is the explosive line, but treating it merely as a personal insult would miss the institutional accusation behind it. Cross’s case is that corporate diversity can change the identity of the person enforcing newsroom discipline without changing who defines acceptable speech or what happens to employees who exceed those boundaries.

Cross said Jones “upheld a lot of the systems in the newsroom that I had a challenge with.” AlterNet reports that executives had become concerned about Cross’s commentary and its frequent departure from MSNBC’s preferred tone. Rival cable hosts and political figures also criticized her style. The network’s response, however, was not controlled by those outside critics. MSNBC’s leadership decided whether their complaints would matter, and the result was the cancellation of The Cross Connection.

The limits of individual blame

Cross did not portray Jones as an all-powerful architect of the corporate order. She described her as someone who learned how to advance within a structure built by and for white executives—and who then enforced that structure from the top.

“There is some level of knowing that they elevate those who they feel comfortable with,” Cross said. She also acknowledged Jones’s ascent from the Weather Channel to leading MSNBC as a substantial professional achievement.

That qualification does not erase Jones’s agency. Cross’s account places Jones inside a hierarchy, but also at the point where institutional preference became an employment decision. Describing executives as products of a system can explain their constraints; it cannot make their decisions ownerless.

Cross nevertheless said she tries to extend Jones “some grace,” arguing that both women were caught in a system that pits Black women against one another. That framing captures a real imbalance: Cross and Jones did not meet as equally situated colleagues in a private dispute. One ran the network; the other depended on it for airtime and employment. Whatever pressures Jones may have faced, Cross absorbed the concrete consequence.

A network’s comfort still sets the boundary

Cross suggested that Jones may have received internal complaints about her reporting style and faced a struggle inside the company. The supplied reporting does not establish what those discussions contained or what Jones privately believed. Cross’s further suggestion that Jones ultimately chose corporate politics over what she thought was right remains Cross’s interpretation, not a documented admission from Jones.

What is established in AlterNet’s account is narrower and more revealing: MSNBC ended Cross’s program amid reported executive concern that her commentary clashed with the network’s preferred style. The recurring focus on “style” shifts attention from the decision-makers to the employee’s manner of speaking. It turns an exercise of corporate power into a personality problem.

Cross’s plantation analogy is severe, and its historical weight should not be diluted into ordinary office friction. But the underlying charge is specific: elite institutions can advertise representational progress while preserving the same internal rules about whose voice is acceptable. In that arrangement, diversity at the top may change the face of authority without redistributing it.

Cross once looked across that hierarchy and thought, as she put it, “Cheers girl, we made it.” MSNBC’s decision supplied the correction. They had both reached prominent positions, but only one of them had the power to decide whether the other remained on the air.

item.title: GOP insider warns of coming chaos as Trump’s ‘blundering purges’ continue
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s answer to a nationwide aviation crisis was that he bore no responsibility. His transportation secretary likewise refused to apologize. According to conservative commentator Charlie Sykes, that response captures an administration stripping expertise from government, elevating loyalty and then assigning blame everywhere except the presidency when essential systems fail. The immediate warning followed an FAA system failure that grounded flights across the country on Friday. AlterNet
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s answer to a nationwide aviation crisis was that he bore no responsibility. His transportation secretary likewise refused to apologize. According to conservative commentator Charlie Sykes, that response captures an administration stripping expertise from government, elevating loyalty and then assigning blame everywhere except the presidency when essential systems fail.

The immediate warning followed an FAA system failure that grounded flights across the country on Friday. AlterNet reports that other technology disruptions followed, culminating Tuesday morning in reports that the National Security Agency’s highly classified communications network was down. The supplied reporting does not establish that the outages shared a cause. Sykes’s argument is narrower and more consequential: an administration conducting what he calls “blundering purges” is weakening its own capacity to prevent crises, manage them and accept responsibility for the results.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Accountability stops at the Oval Office

Trump’s statement after the FAA failure was categorical: “I don’t take any responsibility.” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy similarly said he “can’t apologize,” placing fault elsewhere.

Those remarks are not merely failures of tone. The president appoints senior officials, sets the administration’s priorities and controls the executive branch. When Trump chooses loyalty over experience, responsibility for that governing model belongs to him even when the precise cause of an individual breakdown remains uncertain.

Sykes also faults Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, describing the conduct of Mullin and Duffy as “buffoonery” followed by Trump’s absence, finger-pointing and denials of responsibility. That sequence reveals the political utility of incompetence paired with blame-shifting: officials retain authority while treating accountability as something owed only by people beneath them.

Sykes contrasted that posture with Dwight Eisenhower’s understanding of presidential leadership, quoted in journalist John Dickerson’s The Hardest Job in the World. Eisenhower argued that a leader should assume responsibility when things go wrong and credit subordinates when they go well. Trump’s model reverses the bargain. Power flows upward; fault travels down or outward.

Loyalty remains the governing qualification

Anyone expecting Republican midterm losses to push Trump toward a more competent administration has received the opposite signal. Trump reportedly replaced chief of staff Susie Wiles with longtime adviser Stephen Miller, whom AlterNet describes as a central advocate of several of Trump’s unpopular and politically damaging initiatives.

That personnel decision matters because a chief of staff can impose order, control access to the president and force agencies to confront problems. Installing an ideological loyalist instead reinforces the practice Sykes identifies: expertise is expendable, while personal obedience is indispensable.

Juliette Kayyem, cited by Sykes, suggested that the administration’s “serial faceplants” may show that its management playbook cannot survive the “blue wave.” But electoral punishment does not automatically produce institutional correction. Trump’s reported response has been to intensify the same loyalty-first system. The public absorbs the operational consequences while the people who designed the system protect their positions by denying ownership of it.

A crisis answered with plaster and windows

Asked Monday whether he should remain focused on personal projects during a national crisis, Trump did not explain his administration’s response. He praised work on the White House.

“You take a look at the White House, it’s flawless,” Trump said, before discussing dirt, 18 broken windows and deteriorating exterior plaster that he called “an embarrassment.”

The remark resolved the question more clearly than a prepared statement might have. Confronted with failing public infrastructure, Trump redirected attention to the physical appearance of his own workplace. Flights grounded nationwide became secondary to windows and plaster within the presidential compound.

That is not evidence that Trump caused every reported outage, and the reporting does not claim a demonstrated technical connection among them. It is evidence of how he responds when government failure demands presidential attention: reject responsibility, permit subordinates to do the same and substitute a vanity project for an account of what the administration is doing.

Sykes predicts that conditions will worsen as Trump removes experts and rewards “slavish loyalty over competence and experience.” The exact trajectory remains his assessment. The governing choice beneath it is already visible. Trump holds executive power, selects the loyalists and defends the purges. When the systems under that leadership break, “I don’t take any responsibility” is not an explanation. It is the operating doctrine.

item.title: Alan Dershowitz has candid words for Trump — and a blunt take on free speech
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Alan Dershowitz’s blunt position on free speech is that immigration enforcement does not meaningfully suppress it so long as the person detained or expelled can still speak from somewhere else. In an interview with AlterNet, the former Harvard law professor defended the Trump administration’s treatment of noncitizens, denied that Donald Trump tried to retain power after losing the 2020 election, and endorsed government intervention against public institutions he considers ideological. He objecte
item.content:encoded:
Alan Dershowitz’s blunt position on free speech is that immigration enforcement does not meaningfully suppress it so long as the person detained or expelled can still speak from somewhere else. In an interview with AlterNet, the former Harvard law professor defended the Trump administration’s treatment of noncitizens, denied that Donald Trump tried to retain power after losing the 2020 election, and endorsed government intervention against public institutions he considers ideological. He objected sharply, however, when universities and cultural institutions denied him an audience.

The result is less a coherent defense of free expression than a hierarchy of whose speech counts. Dershowitz treats state custody and exclusion as compatible with liberty, while describing a bookstore’s refusal to stock his book as hostility to the First Amendment. Actual government power recedes from view; private disapproval becomes the emergency.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Speech rights that stop at the border

Asked about Mahmoud Khalil, a green-card holder whom Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained for three months following his criticism of Israel, Dershowitz said he had “no respect for the free speech rights of non-American people.” He argued that the First Amendment applies “in America to Americans” and that a noncitizen removed from the country could continue speaking through Zoom, podcasts or video conferences.

Dershowitz disputed the premise that Khalil had been detained for his speech, saying immigration authorities acted because of Khalil’s status. He also called Khalil a “vicious antisemite,” defining the label broadly enough to include anyone who focuses on Israel and its right to exist without giving comparable attention to the Kurds, Uyghurs or other groups.

That definition does political work. It shifts scrutiny from the government’s use of immigration authority against a critic to the critic’s alleged moral inconsistency. Selective activism may invite criticism, but Dershowitz offered it as a basis for classifying Khalil’s position as antisemitic. The government’s coercive capacity — detention, immigration proceedings and physical control — then becomes administrative background.

His functional test for free speech compounds the evasion. Under it, confinement or removal need not burden expression if technology leaves some channel available. But speech is not preserved merely because a person can theoretically communicate after the state has detained him or forced him elsewhere. Location, legal security and access to an audience are part of political participation, not incidental luxuries.

Dershowitz applied a strikingly different standard to himself. Harvard, New York’s 92nd Street Y and Temple Emanu-El, he said, had effectively banned him from speaking. Because people at those venues could not hear him, he described his free-speech rights as “severely restricted” — even while giving an interview capable of reaching a public audience.

The asymmetry is plain. A noncitizen held by federal agents supposedly retains meaningful freedom because Zoom exists. Dershowitz, free and nationally prominent, portrays rejected speaking invitations as a grave restriction.

The narrowest possible account of 2020

Dershowitz also rejected the suggestion that his defense of Trump during the first impeachment helped embolden the president. In 2020, he argued that an otherwise lawful presidential act did not become impeachable merely because it was partly motivated by reelection. In the AlterNet interview, he stood by that position, saying such a rule could expose virtually any president to impeachment and comparing Trump’s exercises of authority with those of Abraham Lincoln, Thomas Jefferson and Franklin Roosevelt.

When confronted with his 2019 prediction that Trump would not refuse to leave office after an electoral defeat, Dershowitz declared that events had proved him right. Trump ultimately vacated the White House, he said, despite challenging and continuing to criticize the result.

That answer reduces acceptance of an election to one final physical act: leaving the building. It excludes the sustained challenge preceding the transfer of power and makes departure the only relevant test. Dershowitz likewise rejected the interviewer’s description of January 6 as a coup attempt. Trump, he argued, called for lawful protest and did not personally urge illegal conduct or attempt to prevent succession through physical force; those who broke the law acted on their own.

This formulation again narrows responsibility until almost nothing fits inside it. Only an explicit instruction to commit a crime or a personal application of force would apparently count. Political power exercised through rhetoric, pressure or mobilization drops out of the frame. Dershowitz did not merely dispute a label; he adopted a standard that isolates the most powerful actor from the conduct of the people acting in his cause.

Government censorship, selectively defined

Dershowitz blamed the decline of debate largely on Democrats, citing Harvard’s refusal to host a debate with professor Michael Sandel and what he described as efforts to drive Sen. John Fetterman from the party. He also urged listeners not to patronize independent bookstores, alleging that many refuse to carry his book, Why I Quit the Dems: and So Should You!, while stocking only liberal or progressive titles.

He called those businesses “enemies of free speech” and “enemies of the First Amendment.” Yet independent bookstores are not the state. Their purchasing decisions may be narrow, commercially foolish or politically conformist, but they do not wield immigration detention, grant-making authority or control over public institutions. Treating an unwanted book order as constitutionally comparable to government coercion does not clarify free speech. It disguises the power difference at the center of it.

When AlterNet raised Trump administration intervention at the Smithsonian, Dershowitz defended it. He said publicly supported institutions should not promote an ideological account of the United States and agreed with the administration telling the Smithsonian what it could not do. Because the Smithsonian itself is part of the state, he argued, one part of government may restrain another.

That position assigns the administration authority to decide which historical interpretation is objective and which is propaganda. Dershowitz acknowledged that canceling millions of dollars in university research grants was wrong and said he opposed restrictions on “pure science.” But he immediately reopened the door to political defunding when scientists, in his view, use their positions to indoctrinate students. He also approved of defunding National Public Radio and public television on those grounds.

The decisive category is therefore not state interference but Dershowitz’s judgment about the targeted institution. Government restrictions become legitimate correction when he considers the speech ideological; private institutions declining to feature him become censors.

“Debate” as a license for political control

The same instability appeared in the discussion of climate science. Dershowitz said firing people for teaching particular subjects could be wrong, but added that he would want to examine what they taught. He suggested that a professor who presented climate change as beyond dispute or excluded dissenters should be fired. He described the extent of humanity’s effect on the climate as an issue for classroom debate and invoked a creationist applicant as an example of why institutions should admit people with fundamentally contrary views.

There is a defensible principle buried here: education should teach students to examine arguments rather than enforce personal allegiance. Dershowitz described his own goal as helping students think independently, even when they reached conclusions he opposed.

But intellectual openness is not the same as requiring institutions to treat every factual proposition as equally sound. Nor does it explain who should decide when instruction becomes indoctrination. In Dershowitz’s account, that judgment repeatedly migrates upward to officials empowered to remove funding, control exhibits or fire educators.

His advertised commitment to challenge everything thus operates alongside a willingness to let the government punish institutions for conclusions he regards as political. The freedom is expansive for the challenger and conditional for the challenged. It protects Dershowitz’s demand for a platform, but not necessarily a noncitizen’s ability to remain in the country while speaking; it condemns a bookstore’s inventory choices, but tolerates executive control over public history.

Dershowitz told AlterNet that debate is dead. His own argument shows a more specific problem: “debate” can become a flattering name for power deciding which speakers deserve protection, which expertise must be reopened on command and which institutions may be disciplined until they adopt the government’s preferred definition of neutrality.

item.title: Morning Joe unleashes: Get Trump 'off the screen — I don’t want to see him'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Joe Scarborough ordered producers to take President Donald Trump off the screen after Trump aimed a racially loaded insult at a female reporter, suggesting she came from a place where broken windows were unremarkable. The Morning Joe co-host’s eruption was blunt, but the more consequential charge came afterward: Trump’s bigotry persists because Republican voters and officials continue to excuse conduct they would condemn anywhere else. Trump was discussing 18 broken White House windows when he t
item.content:encoded:
Joe Scarborough ordered producers to take President Donald Trump off the screen after Trump aimed a racially loaded insult at a female reporter, suggesting she came from a place where broken windows were unremarkable. The Morning Joe co-host’s eruption was blunt, but the more consequential charge came afterward: Trump’s bigotry persists because Republican voters and officials continue to excuse conduct they would condemn anywhere else.

Trump was discussing 18 broken White House windows when he turned on the reporter. “You never noticed broken windows, obviously, where you come from,” he told her. The remark converted an exchange about property damage into an insinuation about the journalist’s background—and, by extension, the kind of disorder Trump imagined she must consider normal.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

“Get the bigoted comments off,” Scarborough said. “Get him off the screen. I don’t want to see him.”

The insult was presidential conduct, not television provocation

Scarborough rejected the familiar defense that such episodes are merely “Trump being Trump.” That formulation disguises a choice as a personality quirk. Trump chose to answer a reporter by belittling where she supposedly came from, and he did so while exercising the authority and visibility of the presidency.

“That’s the president of the United States being a bigot,” Scarborough said, arguing that Trump repeatedly singles out Black female reporters. He paraphrased the message behind the president’s remark: “I know you’re used to broken glass where you come from.”

Scarborough’s response also exposed the limits of treating Trump’s behavior primarily as offensive television. Cutting away may deny him a broadcast platform in that moment, but it does not remove him from office or diminish the institutional power behind the insult. The central problem is not that viewers were forced to watch an ugly performance. It is that the president used a public exchange to demean a journalist through a stereotype, while members of his party faced the familiar decision of whether to object or accommodate him.

Republicans’ private standards collapse at the ballot box

Scarborough, a former Republican congressman who described his conservative upbringing in the Deep South, focused his criticism on the party’s practiced moral exception for Trump. He said most Republicans would not permit their children to speak that way and would confront another person who did. Yet many vote for a president who does it publicly and then dismiss the result as part of his persona.

That distinction matters. Republican officials and voters are not spectators without leverage. They confer power through nominations, elections, public defenses and silence. When they excuse conduct from a president that they would punish in ordinary life, they are not merely failing to restrain him. They are establishing that partisan utility overrides the standards they claim to hold.

Scarborough’s warning nevertheless remained partly electoral. He argued that Trump’s rhetoric helped drive Black and Hispanic voters toward Democrats and contributed to what he described as major recent Republican defeats. He cited the election of a Black governor in Georgia, a Hispanic woman in Texas and a Black man in Mississippi, along with Democratic gains reaching 56 Senate seats and the possibility that Alaska could also shift.

Those results and projections were presented by Scarborough as evidence for his political diagnosis: that Trump’s bigotry is not only degrading but costly to the party that enables it. He predicted that continued Republican silence could produce a Democratic president and a filibuster-proof Senate majority of 60 or more seats in 2028.

Electoral punishment is not moral accountability

Scarborough’s case becomes narrower when the objection to presidential bigotry rests on how many seats Republicans may lose. The conduct does not become unacceptable only when Black and Hispanic voters punish the party responsible for tolerating it. Nor should the burden of enforcing minimal standards fall on the people targeted by the president’s rhetoric.

Still, his account identifies the operative power structure. Trump delivered the insult. Republican voters and officeholders retain the capacity to impose political consequences. Scarborough’s own forecast assumes that many will act only when the electoral price becomes impossible to ignore.

That is the bleak bargain beneath “Trump being Trump”: the president is granted permission to degrade people until the damage reaches his allies. Scarborough wanted the image removed from the screen. What his own argument showed is that the machinery sustaining it remains firmly in view.

item.title: Judge rejects DOJ’s plea not to delay shut down of federal prosecutor
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright refused. The dispute is not merely about Essayli’s job title: prosecutors acknowledged that the appointment fight could touch 5,000 cases in the nation’s largest federal district, while offering the court no support for that sweeping claim of harm. Essayli was never c
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department tried to keep Bill Essayli in control of federal prosecutions across seven Southern and Central California counties after a judge ruled that his authority had expired. U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright refused. The dispute is not merely about Essayli’s job title: prosecutors acknowledged that the appointment fight could touch 5,000 cases in the nation’s largest federal district, while offering the court no support for that sweeping claim of harm.

Essayli was never confirmed by the Senate. After the 120-day limit on his service as interim U.S. attorney expired, he remained atop the office under a different designation—First Assistant U.S. Attorney. That maneuver preserved the White House’s preferred prosecutor without securing the approval the appointment process requires.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A title change cannot erase a legal deadline

Federal law limits how long an unconfirmed interim U.S. attorney may serve. Once that period ends, a district court can appoint a replacement. Essayli’s continued leadership under a new title attempted to maintain the same practical arrangement after its statutory clock ran out.

The issue reached Seabright through criminal proceedings involving Jaime Hector Ramirez, charged with unlawful firearm possession, and Tu Anh Tran, accused of possessing property stolen from an interstate or foreign shipment. Defense attorney Dean Steward, representing Tran, challenged Essayli’s authority while seeking reconsideration of a motion to dismiss the charges. He also sought Essayli’s disqualification.

Seabright had previously allowed Essayli to remain as first assistant. He reconsidered after the Ninth Circuit disqualified Nevada prosecutor Sigal Chattah in a similar dispute. Courts have also rejected Trump administration arrangements for installing or retaining prosecutors in New Jersey and Virginia, although those cases involved different appointment histories and legal questions.

That emerging pattern matters. An administration cannot treat Senate confirmation and statutory time limits as optional obstacles, then preserve the same official’s power through creative relabeling. The executive chooses nominees; it does not get to rewrite the conditions governing how long an unconfirmed choice may wield prosecutorial authority.

The department invoked 5,000 cases without substantiating the danger

The Justice Department asked Seabright to delay the practical effect of his ruling while Essayli appealed to the Ninth Circuit. Yet, according to the judge, the government conceded that it would suffer no injury from Essayli’s immediate removal from the Ramirez and Tran cases.

Instead, prosecutors raised a broader institutional objection. Seabright wrote that the government claimed a court had displaced the executive’s preferred official and reassigned supervision of criminal prosecutors using a theory it said no other court had applied. That is a separation-of-powers argument, but it also reverses the relevant sequence: the conflict arose because the administration kept its chosen prosecutor in command after the deadline for his unconfirmed appointment.

Prosecutors then said, “for the first time,” that the ruling could affect 5,000 cases. Seabright rejected the claim as a “bald assertion” offered without explanation or support, finding that it did not establish probable irreparable injury.

The number functions less as a demonstrated consequence than as institutional leverage. The department invoked the possible disruption of thousands of prosecutions to resist the immediate enforcement of appointment rules it had tried to route around. If those cases face uncertainty, that uncertainty did not originate with defendants questioning lawful authority. It arose from the executive branch’s decision to entrust prosecutorial power to an official whose legal tenure was vulnerable.

Criminal defendants bear the risk of the appointment maneuver

At the time of the report, the Ramirez and Tran trials were scheduled for the following week, and Essayli had appealed Seabright’s ruling. The Ninth Circuit’s earlier decision against Chattah gives that appeal an especially relevant backdrop, though it does not by itself dictate the result because the cases are not identical.

The immediate stakes belong to defendants facing federal prosecution and to cases that may be challenged over who lawfully supervised them. Prosecutorial authority is coercive state power: it determines which charges advance, how cases are managed and when the government attempts to take away a person’s liberty. The rules governing that authority are not clerical formalities.

The Justice Department’s argument asks the court to prioritize continuity after the administration created a continuity problem. Seabright declined to let an unsupported warning about 5,000 cases substitute for a showing of concrete injury. Essayli’s title changed; the underlying exercise of power did not. That is precisely why the court’s scrutiny became unavoidable.

item.title: Ex-prosecutor exposes the bluff behind Trump ally’s criminal threats
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The criminal threat was a bluff, according to former U.S. Attorney Joyce Vance: Aaron Reitz, the Trump-appointed U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, warned four Democratic lawmakers that their planned oversight might violate federal law even though none falls within his district and no public record cited by Vance shows that the attorney general authorized him to operate elsewhere. item.content:encoded:
The criminal threat was a bluff, according to former U.S. Attorney Joyce Vance: Aaron Reitz, the Trump-appointed U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, warned four Democratic lawmakers that their planned oversight might violate federal law even though none falls within his district and no public record cited by Vance shows that the attorney general authorized him to operate elsewhere. The letters did not announce charges or reveal a conventional criminal investigation. They used the authority of a federal prosecutor’s office to place a legal cloud over lawmakers preparing to scrutinize the Trump administration.

A prosecutor reaches beyond his jurisdiction

Reitz sent what he called “preservation letters” to Rep. Robert Garcia of California and Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. All four intend to assume oversight roles involving the administration in January.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The letters instructed them to retain records concerning their alleged “intention to weaponize congressional investigations” and suggested that they could be committing two federal civil-rights crimes. That framing turns congressional scrutiny into the suspected offense before the oversight has even begun. It also adopts the administration’s political accusation—“weaponization”—as though it were already a legal theory.

Vance argued in her Civil Discourse newsletter that Reitz lacks the authority to make good on the implied threat. Federal law generally confines U.S. attorneys to their own districts unless the attorney general gives them a broader assignment, she wrote, and no such designation for Reitz has been made public. The distinction is not academic. In 2019, Attorney General William Barr expressly appointed John Durham to investigate the origins of the Russia inquiry.

Vance also cited the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals’ ruling in Ghislaine Maxwell’s case, which found that Jeffrey Epstein’s agreement with federal prosecutors in Florida did not bind prosecutors elsewhere. Federal prosecutorial power is divided geographically; an official in Texas does not acquire national jurisdiction by mailing threatening correspondence.

Oversight recast as a civil-rights crime

The threatened charges appear no sturdier than the jurisdictional claim. Vance wrote that prosecutors would need to establish that the lawmakers intended to deprive someone of a federally protected right. Requests for information in the course of congressional oversight do not, by themselves, supply that intent. She further argued that the First Amendment and the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause would protect the lawmakers’ activity.

That matters because Reitz’s letters do more than preserve possible evidence. They invert the relationship between Congress and the executive branch. The lawmakers are preparing to investigate an administration; an administration-appointed prosecutor has responded by suggesting that the investigators themselves may be criminals.

Blumenthal’s letter centered largely on his inquiry into donors connected to the White House ballroom. His Nov. 11 response was direct: “I will not be intimidated.”

Vance noted that a prosecutor conducting an actual criminal investigation would ordinarily use grand-jury subpoenas, not public-facing preservation letters of this kind. Her assessment was that Reitz’s move appeared political. His résumé reinforces the relevance of that question: before becoming U.S. attorney, he served as chief of staff to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz and came from a policy background rather than a prosecutorial one. That history does not prove improper conduct, but it supplies important context for a legal warning built around an overtly partisan accusation.

The threat was also a performance

President Donald Trump amplified Reitz’s posts about the letters on Truth Social, including one declaring, “My first arrow shot.” The publicity clarifies the letters’ immediate political function regardless of whether they could support a prosecution: they allowed an administration ally to portray prospective oversight as unlawful and Trump to broadcast that warning to his audience.

A quiet evidence-preservation step does not require presidential promotion or martial branding. Those choices transformed official correspondence into political theater backed by the implied coercive force of the Justice Department. The point was not merely to notify four lawmakers. It was to demonstrate that investigating the administration could make an investigator a target.

The performance may now carry professional consequences for Reitz. On Monday, the Campaign for Accountability filed a grievance with the State Bar of Texas concerning the letters sent to Blumenthal and Warren, according to Democracy Docket. A bar complaint is not a finding of misconduct, but it moves scrutiny toward the official who invoked criminal law—not the lawmakers whose planned oversight he tried to cast as a crime.

Reitz called the letters his first arrow. On the facts presented by Vance, he appears to have fired it outside his jurisdiction, at constitutionally protected congressional work, with a criminal theory she argues cannot reach its target. What remains is the intimidation: a federal office used to make unsupported legal peril part of the cost of investigating the president.

item.title: Psychotherapist details what Trump’s angry outburst reveals about his brain
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A psychotherapist’s viral-style analysis of Donald Trump’s angry exchange with a reporter does not establish that Trump has Alzheimer’s disease, dementia or any other neurological disorder. It establishes that Elliott Connie watched Trump snap at a question, heard a disjointed answer and interpreted both as signs of cognitive decline. AlterNet nevertheless packaged that interpretation as a revelation about the president’s brain—a certainty the reported facts cannot support. The episode raises a
item.content:encoded:
A psychotherapist’s viral-style analysis of Donald Trump’s angry exchange with a reporter does not establish that Trump has Alzheimer’s disease, dementia or any other neurological disorder. It establishes that Elliott Connie watched Trump snap at a question, heard a disjointed answer and interpreted both as signs of cognitive decline. AlterNet nevertheless packaged that interpretation as a revelation about the president’s brain—a certainty the reported facts cannot support.

The episode raises a legitimate question about presidential capacity. But Connie’s attempt to answer it remotely, then speculate that undisclosed medical treatment kept Trump from public view during a nationwide aviation disruption, substitutes clinical-sounding conjecture for evidence. It also shifts attention away from what the exchange plainly showed: a president responding with hostility when asked how he was allocating his time during a crisis.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A question about priorities met with an outburst

Before leaving Monday for meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, Trump took questions from reporters. One asked whether he was spending too much time on renovation projects while more serious matters demanded attention, including the nationwide ground stop for aircraft the previous Friday.

Trump said the construction work consumed only “10 minutes per day.” According to Connie, Trump then defended the projects by pointing to the White House’s appearance, its stonework and a helipad. Connie described the answer as “extremely disjointed” and likened Trump’s enthusiasm to a child seeking approval for a new toy.

The political issue does not depend on that analogy. A reporter asked the president to account for his priorities during a major disruption. Trump’s answer, as described by AlterNet, turned toward the beauty and importance of his renovations. His anger and deflection are matters of observable conduct. Whether a neurological condition caused them is not.

That distinction matters because presidents exercise power through decisions, attention and delegation—not through a public performance that must first be medically decoded before it can be judged. If Trump neglected a crisis, the relevant questions concern what he did, what his administration did and who was responsible. A speculative diagnosis can blur that line of accountability by recasting chosen behavior as a symptom.

Clinical language outruns the evidence

Connie, identified as a practicing psychotherapist of 20 years, argued in a Tuesday video that Trump’s behavior was more than disrespectful or “non-presidential.” He called it evidence of cognitive decline or neurological disruption associated with advancing Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

His explanation centered on the prefrontal cortex, which he described as the brain’s “mental stop sign”—the mechanism that restrains a person from acting on every irritated impulse. Connie contended that Trump’s angry responses show this system deteriorating. AlterNet also said clinical and forensic psychologist John Paul Garrison had noticed something concerning in Trump’s eye contact, though the supplied report does not detail Garrison’s conclusion.

None of that turns an observed outburst into a diagnosis. Irritability, rambling and poor impulse control may prompt questions, but the article reports no examination by Connie and no medical finding from Trump’s treating clinicians. Connie’s professional credentials do not erase the evidentiary gap between watching a press exchange and determining what is happening inside a person’s brain.

The headline’s promised revelation therefore exceeds the story. What the outburst “reveals” about Trump’s brain is Connie’s interpretation, not an established medical fact.

Speculation becomes an alibi

Connie went further. He said he believed Trump was probably receiving medical treatment that affected his speech, gait and general functioning, requiring aides to keep him from cameras until he could appear publicly again. He offered that theory as “the most likely reason” Trump was absent while flights were grounded.

AlterNet’s account provides no factual basis for that conclusion beyond Connie’s reading of Trump’s public behavior. The claim must remain what it is: one psychotherapist’s speculation about treatment he was not reported to have witnessed and a presidential schedule he was not reported to control.

That speculation is not merely medically tenuous. It redirects responsibility from the institution with the power to answer. If the president was unavailable during a nationwide aviation emergency, the White House can account for his whereabouts and role. If officials concealed a health problem affecting his capacity, that would be an institutional act requiring evidence. If Trump simply devoted his attention elsewhere, that would be a political choice. Guessing at secret treatment resolves none of those possibilities.

Connie concluded that the country must be honest about the president’s health and capacity because, in his view, Trump is “unwell.” Scrutiny of presidential fitness is warranted precisely because the office carries extraordinary power. But serious scrutiny requires more discipline than converting belligerence into a brain scan and absence into proof of hidden care.

Trump’s reported conduct already supplies a concrete basis for judgment: confronted about his priorities during a national disruption, he lashed out and promoted his construction projects. Turning that documented exercise of power into an unsupported neurological story does not sharpen accountability. It gives the president’s behavior a speculative medical explanation when the available facts support a simpler political question: why did the man holding the office answer a crisis-management challenge by demanding admiration for his stones and helipad?
